local_facts.claim: Colorado law makes irretrievable breakdown of the marriage relationship the sole basis for dissolution. A petition for dissolution must allege that the marriage is irretrievably broken.
local_facts.why_it_matters: The statutory basis for a Colorado divorce is different from proving marital misconduct. That rule does not resolve the separate questions about property, debt, parenting, support, disclosures, or an agreement in a particular case.
local_facts.title: Colorado’s divorce standard is irretrievable breakdown

local_facts.claim: Colorado Judicial Branch instructions say a divorce has a 91-day waiting period even if spouses agree on all issues. The period begins when a joint petition is filed, or when the other spouse is served or signs a waiver in a separately filed matter.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Ninety-one days is a minimum court period, not a promise that a case will be finished on that date. Filing, service, financial documents, court directions, agreements, disagreements, and scheduling can affect the path after a case begins.
local_facts.title: The 91-day period is a minimum, not a completion date

local_facts.claim: Denver District Court handles domestic-relations cases, including dissolution of marriage. Colorado’s filing instructions say each spouse must file a Sworn Financial Statement and Certificate of Compliance within 42 days after filing or receiving the petition; Denver also publishes local family-law forms for use in Denver District Court only.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A Denver matter can involve both statewide Colorado requirements and Denver-only court materials. Organizing financial records and checking the correct court’s instructions helps prevent a form or timing detail from being overlooked.
local_facts.title: Denver cases use statewide rules and Denver court materials
